{{3D computer graphics}}

In [[3D computer graphics]], the '''image plane''', also called '''screen space''', is that [[Euclidean planes in three-dimensional space|plane in the world]] which corresponds to the [[display monitor]] used to view the image that is being [[3D rendering|rendered]]. If one makes the analogy of taking a [[photograph]] to [[Rendering (computer graphics)|rendering]] a 3D image, the surface of the [[Photographic film|film]] (or the [[image sensor]]) is the image plane. In this case, the [[viewing transformation]] is a [[3D projection|projection]] that maps the world onto the image plane. A rectangular region of this plane, called the viewing window or [[viewport]], maps to the monitor. This establishes the mapping between [[pixels]] on the monitor and points (or rather, [[Ray (geometry)|rays]]) in the 3D world. The plane is not usually an actual [[geometric object]] in a [[3D scene]], but instead is usually a collection of target coordinates or dimensions that are used during the [[rasterization]] process so the final output can be displayed as intended on the physical screen.

In [[optics]], the image plane is the plane that contains the object's projected image, and lies beyond the back [[focal plane]].<ref name=PHIP1>{{cite web|url=http://www.photokonnexion.com/definition-focal-plane-film-plane/|title=Definition: Focal Plane; Image Plane; Film Plane; Sensor plane|access-date=18 November 2017}}</ref>
